title: Fallen Angels and the Watchers
lead: The Bible speaks of angels who rebelled against God, but it says little about how. Genesis 6:1–4, Jewish tradition about the "Watchers," and a few New Testament verses gave rise to very different accounts.

sections.h: The sons of God in Genesis 6
sections.b: "The sons of God saw that the daughters of humankind were good to look at, and they took wives for themselves" (Genesis 6:2). The Nephilim were on the earth in those days. Elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, "sons of God" are heavenly beings (Job 1:6; 38:7). Most Jewish readers before about AD 100 took Genesis 6 to mean angels, as 1 Enoch does. From the 100s and 200s others disagreed: Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai read "sons of nobles" (Genesis Rabbah 26:5), Targum Onqelos "sons of the great ones," and Julius Africanus (about 220) the godly line of Seth, a view Augustine made standard in the West.

A separate tradition, built from Isaiah 14:12–15 ("How you have fallen from the heavens, Shining One, son of Dawn"), Ezekiel 28:12–17 and Revelation 12:7–9, pictures Satan and his angels falling in a primeval rebellion. Isaiah and Ezekiel speak in their contexts of the kings of Babylon and Tyre; many Christian interpreters have also seen in them the devil's fall, while others think that goes beyond the texts.
